title: What should you ask first in a market sizing case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a market sizing case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first what exactly you are sizing: units or value, which geography and period, and what is in scope. The trap to avoid is launching into multiplication with no rough guess to aim at and no cross-check at the end. The routine below works whether the sizing question stands alone or turns up in the middle of a bigger case.
body:
The first questions to ask

"Before I start: are we sizing units or value? Which country, and over what period? And is that consumers only, or businesses too?"

Each of these can change the answer by a factor of two or more. "Coffee machines sold in the UK this year, in dollars" and "coffee machines in UK homes" are different questions. If the sizing sits inside a bigger case, add one more question: what decision will this number inform? If the client only needs to know whether the market is above $100M, a rough answer is enough.

The routine

  1. Clarify units, geography, period and scope.
  2. Say a rough guess (your hypothesis): "probably a few hundred million dollars".
  3. Choose a side: buyers (demand) or sellers (supply). See which side to start from.
  4. Segment where it matters, and use round numbers, saying that you are rounding.
  5. Sanity-check from another direction: the other side, a per-person figure, or a number you know.
  6. Land it: give a rounded answer, name the assumption that drives it, and say what it means for the client.

The trap most people fall into

Going straight into the maths. Without a rough guess, you cannot tell when an answer is ten times too big. Without a cross-check, you cannot show the interviewer that it is not. Both take under 30 seconds, and they are what separates a calculation from a judgement.

A close second trap is confusing stock and flow: the number of things in use (phones, tyres, umbrellas) versus the number bought each year. If the question says "per year", divide the stock by how long the item lasts.

An example

"How big is the UK market for dog grooming?"

  • Clarify: value, per year, UK, professional grooming only (not shampoo bought for home use).
  • Guess: a few hundred million dollars.
  • Build: about 11M pet dogs in the UK (PDSA estimated about 10.6M in 2024). Assume 30% are professionally groomed, 4 times a year, at $50 a visit: 11M × 30% × 4 × $50 = $660M a year.
  • Check: $660M ÷ 11M dogs = $60 per dog per year across all dogs, or $200 a year for each groomed dog. Both feel plausible. From the supply side, 13.2M visits at 6 dogs a day per groomer over 250 days means about 8,800 groomers, which sounds like a believable national trade.
  • Land it: "Roughly $650M a year. The share of dogs groomed professionally is the assumption I would test first."

How it sounds in an interview

"Before I size it, my rough guess is a few hundred million dollars. I'll build it from the number of dogs and check it against what an owner spends in a year and how many groomers that would need."

Quick practice

The interviewer asks: "How big is the e-bike market in the Netherlands?" What do you ask before you start?

Show the answer

Units or value? New e-bikes only, or used too? Bikes only, or also batteries, servicing and accessories? One year? And why the client wants to know: a maker deciding whether to enter needs annual new sales by value, while a repair chain needs the number of e-bikes in use.
